titulo: Why does rain smell like that?
fuentes: Bear & Thomas, Nature (1964), 'Nature of Argillaceous Odour': coined the term 'petrichor' (CSIRO, Australia)
Geosmin: compound produced by soil bacteria (mainly Streptomyces); humans detect it at a few parts per trillion

MIT, Joung & Buie, Nature Communications (2015), 'Aerosol generation by raindrop impact on soil': drops trap air bubbles that burst and release aerosols; more with light to moderate rain than heavy rain
Evolutionary idea about human sensitivity to geosmin (finding water): a hypothesis, not conclusive
destinatario: se lo manda alguien a su amigo que sale al porche, respira hondo y dice 'ah, olor a lluvia'
receta: experimento real con fuente en pantalla (MIT 2015)

frases.texto: That smell when it starts to rain? It isn't the rain.
frases.estilo: Dry and confident, with a half smile.

frases.texto: A big part of it comes from the ground, including a chemical made by soil bacteria.
It has a name: petrichor. Two Australian scientists coined it in nineteen sixty-four.
One key ingredient is a molecule called geosmin, made by soil bacteria.
frases.estilo: Explaining simply, like to a friend.

frases.texto: When a raindrop hits dry ground, it traps tiny air bubbles that pop and release aerosols. MIT researchers filmed it in twenty fifteen, and think it may help carry the scent.
And your nose is so sharp, it can pick up geosmin at just a few parts per trillion.
Why? One idea is that our ancestors followed that smell to find water.
frases.estilo: Curious, as a theory, not a certainty.

frases.texto: Heads up: in MIT's tests, light to moderate rain released more aerosols than a downpour.
Next time it starts to drizzle, step outside and take a deep breath.
Send this to the friend who steps onto the porch and says, ah, rain smell.
frases.estilo: Playful, with humor, as a punchline.
